subject: chemistry
question_text: Explain why graphite is a lubricant.

verification.note: Source: Sri Chaitanya, IPE STUDY MATERIAL for Jr. Students — Chemistry (2026-27 edition), book p.107, chapter 9 p-BLOCK ELEMENTS GROUP 14, Short Answer Questions question 32(c). Only the question was taken. The solution, the step order and the mark split are this answer book's own work — see docs/ORIGINALITY_MATHS.md. THE MARK SPLIT IS OURS, NOT THE BOOK'S: the volume prints no per-step allocation on any answer in this chapter. The book prints no exam-appearance years for this question, so appearances[] is empty. This is the four-mark form of a question the chapter also asks at two marks; the extra marks here are spent on the structure that causes the sliding — the sp² sheets, the bond length and angle inside a sheet, and the contrast between the two directions — and on where a dry lubricant is used, not on restating the sliding. BOND LENGTH: the source book prints the graphite C–C distance as 141.5 pm in one place and as 1.42 Å in two others; those are the same value rounded differently, and this card prints 141.5 pm only. Neither form is an error. This is a coaching publication, not a TSBIE document, so the split stays unverified until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it.

steps.label: The structure of graphite
lines: In graphite each carbon atom is sp²
hybridised and is joined to three other
carbon atoms by strong sigma bonds.
These bonds build flat sheets of
hexagonal rings.
Inside a sheet the C–C bond length is
141.5 pm and the bond angle is 120°.
The fourth valence electron of each
carbon is delocalised over the sheet.
steps.why: The answer has to start with the structure, because everything about the lubrication follows from it. The sp² bonding is what makes the sheets flat, and a flat sheet is the shape that can slide over another flat sheet.
common_mistakes: Answering sp³ for graphite. Each carbon is joined to three others, so it is sp².
Describing graphite as a three-dimensional network. That is diamond; graphite is built of separate flat sheets.
steps.memory_tip: sp² carbon, three bonds, flat hexagonal sheets at 120°.
steps.margin_note: Start with the structure. A description of the sliding with no structure behind it is only half the answer.

steps.label: The forces between the sheets
lines: The sheets are stacked one above
another.
Nothing joins one sheet to the next
except weak van der Waals forces, and
the sheets lie much further apart than
the carbon atoms within a sheet.
So the crystal is strongly bonded in
two directions and only weakly held in
the third.
steps.why: This contrast between the two directions is the main point. A crystal that is strong along its sheets and weak across them can be pulled apart in one direction only, and that single weak direction is what a lubricant needs.
common_mistakes: Writing that the sheets are covalently bonded to each other. If they were, graphite could not slide and would not be soft.
Saying the layers are held by metallic bonds. Graphite is a non-metal; the forces between the sheets are van der Waals forces.
steps.memory_tip: Strong in two directions, weak in the third.
steps.margin_note: Say in words that the two directions are different; that contrast is the argument.

steps.label: Why the sheets slide
lines: A small sideways force is enough to
overcome the weak forces between the
sheets, so one sheet slides over the
next.
The strong sigma bonds inside each
sheet are not broken while this
happens, so the sheets stay whole.
Graphite is therefore soft and greasy
to the touch, and it marks paper, which
is why it is used in pencil leads.
steps.why: Two facts have to sit side by side here: the sheets move, and the sheets stay whole. If the sheets broke as well, graphite would crumble away instead of lasting as a lubricating film.
common_mistakes: Writing that the covalent bonds break when graphite is used. Only the weak forces between the sheets are overcome.
Saying graphite is soft because it has a low melting point. Its melting point is high; the softness comes from the sliding sheets.
steps.memory_tip: The sheets move but do not break.
steps.margin_note: State both halves: the sheets slide, and the bonds inside them hold.

steps.label: Graphite as a lubricant

lines.text: Sliding sheets make graphite a lubricant

lines: Powdered graphite spread between two
moving metal surfaces forms thin sheets
that slide over one another, so the
metal surfaces move with less friction
and wear away more slowly.
Graphite is a dry lubricant, so it can
be used at temperatures at which an oil
would decompose, and in machinery where
an oil film would collect dust.
steps.why: A reason has to end in the thing it explains. Naming the two places a dry lubricant is chosen — high temperature and dusty machinery — turns the structural argument into an answer about lubrication.
common_mistakes: Describing the structure and never using the word lubricant. The question asks for the use, so the answer has to reach it.
Writing that graphite lubricates because it is a good conductor. Conduction and lubrication come from two different parts of the structure.
steps.memory_tip: A dry lubricant works where oil would burn away or trap dust.
steps.margin_note: One closing line naming the use completes the answer.

insider_note: A complete answer works downwards from the structure: flat sp² sheets, weak van der Waals forces between them, sheets sliding under a small force, and only then the word lubricant with a place it is used.
